meta.title: Forward Deployed Engineer
meta.sub: The engineer who builds the solution on-site with the client
meta.short: Goes to the client and builds AI into their work so it actually makes money.
meta.intro: A regular developer builds a product for thousands of customers. A Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) works with one client: sits next to their people, finds where the product will pay off, writes the integration code, ships it to production, and brings back to their own company whatever the product is missing. The role was invented at Palantir, and once large language models arrived, almost every company selling AI to businesses built teams like this: a model on its own changes nothing until it is built into the client's processes.
traits: Talks to the client every day
Owns the outcome, not just the task
Gets up to speed in someone else's industry fast

role.title: Understand the role
role.why: An FDE is a mix of developer, consultant, and product manager. First, figure out what you're signing up for: this is not "a programmer who sometimes calls the client."
role.project: Pick an industry you know for your end-to-end project, like logistics, a clinic, or a store. Describe on one page who the client is, what hurts, and what changes once that pain is gone.

code.title: Programming foundations
code.why: An FDE writes a lot of code, fast, inside unfamiliar systems. You need solid Python, the ability to read other people's code, and comfort in the terminal.
code.project: Create a GitHub repository for the project. Write a Python script that reads a client data export (CSV) and prints the three key numbers from it.

data.title: Data
data.why: The value of AI for a client lives in their data. And that data is always messy: mixed formats, duplicates, Excel files with merged cells. An FDE spends most of their time here.
data.project: Load your project data into PostgreSQL. Describe the schema and write 5 SQL queries that answer the "client's" questions.

integr.title: Backend and integrations
integr.why: An FDE's solution almost never lives on its own: it pulls data from the CRM, writes to the ERP, and lets users in through corporate sign-on. Integrations are most of the code.
integr.project: Wrap your project logic in a FastAPI service: one endpoint takes a question, another returns a report. Add API key authentication.

cloud.title: Cloud and deployment
cloud.why: A prototype on your laptop is not a result. An FDE ships the solution to the cloud or into the client's closed network, where there may be no internet at all.
cloud.project: Package the service in Docker and deploy it to the cloud with automatic deployment from GitHub on every push to main.

ai.title: AI systems engineering
ai.why: Today most FDEs ship solutions built on large language models. Knowing how to call an API isn't enough: you need reliable quality on the client's data and numbers to prove it.
ai.project: Build an AI assistant that answers questions from the "client's" documents and database, with links to sources. Put together a set of 50 questions with correct answers and measure accuracy.

prod.title: Production
prod.why: The solution has to keep working after you leave. That means you can see what's happening inside it, it survives failures in neighboring systems, and it comes with documentation.
prod.project: Add logs with a request ID, a dashboard with key metrics, and an on-call guide: "what to do if…".

client.title: Working with the client
client.why: Half of an FDE's job is people. Technically strong engineers most often fail right here: they build the wrong thing, stay quiet about risks, or can't show the result.
client.project: Run 3 interviews with people from your chosen industry about their routine. Rewrite the project goal based on what you learn and demo it to one of them.

domain.title: The client's industry
domain.why: After a month with a client, an FDE should speak the language of their industry. Strong FDEs eventually become experts in one or two industries.
domain.project: Build a glossary of 30 terms for your industry and a map of its core process (for example, an order's path from request to payment).

career.title: Portfolio and getting hired
career.why: FDEs get hired for the projects they've built and how they think. A resume listing technologies barely matters.
career.project: Polish your end-to-end project: a README with the client's problem, the architecture and quality numbers, a 3-minute demo video, and a story about what went wrong.

role-what.what: An engineer sent straight to the client so the company's technology actually works for them: half programmer, half translator between AI and business.
learn: How an FDE differs from a regular product developer
Why AI you bought changes nothing without integration and the client's data
Where FDEs work: on-site, remotely, on business trips

role-work.what: A project runs in a cycle: kickoff and scope, prototype, pilot, production, and handoff to the client's team, with feedback flowing back into the product.
learn: The cycle: kickoff → prototype → pilot → production → handoff
How success is measured: time, money, quality
How an FDE differs from a Solutions Engineer and a consultant

role-pay.what: FDE is one of the best-paid engineering roles: income includes base salary, bonuses, and equity, and the level depends heavily on the country and the company.
learn: What income is made of: salary, bonus, stock
How to compare annual and monthly numbers
Why salaries differ several times over between countries

role-traits.what: The role gives fast growth and visible results, but it means travel, work without clear requirements, and constant communication. It's not for everyone.
learn: Pros: growth, impact, variety of work
Qualities that matter more than the stack: ownership, clear speaking, speed

role-day.t: A day in the life of an FDE
role-day.what: An FDE's day is questions for the client's staff, code, checking quality on real examples, and a short status update in the evening.
learn: Why you ask about yesterday's work, not about wishes
How to measure solution quality with numbers
What a typical workday at the client looks like

role-code.t: Your first code at a client
role-code.what: The first code is usually small: read the client's export, clean it, ask the model, and save the result, but do it safely and reliably.
learn: A small pipeline: read → clean → ask the model → save
Why you clean data before sending it to the model
Access keys never in the code; timeouts always

role-future.what: Some of the routine will go to machines, but understanding the client, framing the problem, and owning the result will stay human work, and that's where FDE career paths come from.
learn: What in FDE work gets automated first
Where to grow: architect, team lead, industry expert, your own product

py.what: The FDE's main language: integrations, data processing, and almost everything around AI models are written in it. You need a level where the language doesn't get in the way of thinking about the problem.
learn: Working with files, JSON, CSV, dates, and time zones
py.practice: Write a command-line tool that takes a path to a folder of CSV files, merges them, removes duplicates, and saves a report.
check: How is a list different from a generator, and when does it matter?
How do you isolate the dependencies of two projects on one machine?

ts.what: Client-facing interfaces like demos, internal dashboards, and chats are most often written in TypeScript. You need to be able to put together a clear screen quickly, not become a frontend architect.
learn: Node.js: running scripts and a simple server
One framework at a basic level (React or Next.js)
ts.practice: Build a page that shows the output of your Python script as a table and a chart.
check: What does fetch return if the server responds with 500: an error or a response?

git.what: All the code at a client lives in repositories, often the client's own, with their own rules. You need to branch confidently, resolve conflicts, and write clear pull requests.
learn: What must never end up in a repo: keys and personal data
git.practice: Create a branch in your project, make changes, and open a pull request with a description: what, why, how to test.
check: How do you remove an accidentally committed key from history, and what do you do with the key itself?

shell.what: Client servers are almost always Linux, often with no graphical interface and limited access. You need to find logs, a process, and the cause of an error using only the terminal.
shell.practice: Connect to any cloud server over ssh and find the last 20 errors in the logs with a single command.
check: How do you find out which process is using port 8080?

http.what: Almost every integration is HTTP requests between systems. An FDE should read a request and response as plain text and immediately see what went wrong.
learn: Postman, curl, the Network tab in the browser
http.practice: Call a public API three ways: curl, Python (httpx), and Postman. Break the request and figure out the error.
check: How is 401 different from 403?
Why can retrying a POST request create a duplicate?

debug.t: Reading other people's code and debugging
debug.what: At a client you constantly land in someone else's systems with no documentation. The key skill is quickly understanding unfamiliar code and finding the cause of a failure.
learn: The debugger: breakpoints, stepping through code
Logs as the first source of truth
Binary search for the cause: what changed and when
A minimal reproduction of the bug
debug.practice: Take any open-source project on GitHub, find an issue describing a bug, and reproduce it locally.
check: Where do you start if "everything broke at the client" and nothing else is known?

sql.what: The language all corporate data speaks. You need it to the point where you calmly write a query with several JOINs, groupings, and window functions.
sql.practice: Find the top 10 customers by revenue for each month in a single query.
check: Why can a LEFT JOIN unexpectedly multiply rows?

model.what: To build a product in, you need to understand how the client's entities are structured: order, contract, patient, shipment. A bad data model breaks everything built on top of it.
learn: Normalization and when to break it
How to read someone else's database schema in an hour
model.practice: Draw a data schema for a fictional clinic: patients, doctors, appointments, lab tests.
check: How do you store a product's price if it changes over time?

wrangle.what: Fast analysis and cleanup of the exports the client sends you. It lets you answer "what's actually in this data" within an hour.
learn: Excel and CSV in different encodings
Simple charts for conversations with the client
wrangle.practice: Take a "messy" Excel file with merged cells and turn it into a clean table.
check: How do you find duplicates when names are written differently ("Alpha LLC" and "LLC Alpha")?

etl.what: A one-off export is a prototype. In production, data has to arrive on its own every day, and the system has to notice when it breaks.
learn: Quality checks: empty fields, outliers, duplicates
etl.practice: Write a script that pulls new rows every hour and logs a warning if no data arrived.
check: What happens to the report if loading fails halfway? How do you prevent that?

docs.what: A huge share of a client's knowledge lives not in databases but in contracts, manuals, emails, and scans. It's the main data source for AI assistants.
learn: Extracting text from PDF and Word
docs.practice: Extract text and tables from 20 different PDFs and count how many came out without errors.
check: How do you tell which of two contract versions is the one in force?

api.what: For the client's systems to use your solution, it has to be a service with a clear API.
api.practice: Build a service with three endpoints and auto-generated docs, and cover them with tests.
check: How do you change an API without breaking the people already using it?

auth.what: In a corporation nobody creates new passwords: people sign in through corporate single sign-on (SSO), and systems use tokens. A mistake here is a security problem for the client.
learn: API keys and how to store them
SSO with Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Okta
auth.practice: Add Google or Microsoft sign-in to your service.
check: Why shouldn't you keep a token in the code, or in localStorage unless you have to?

events.what: Client systems report events in different ways: webhooks, queues, sometimes an email. A reliable integration never loses events and never processes them twice.
events.practice: Receive a webhook, put the event in a queue, and process it in a separate worker.
check: What happens if your service was down for 10 minutes while webhooks kept coming?

enterprise.what: CRM, ERP, accounting systems, SharePoint: that's where the client's data lives. They often have awkward APIs, rate limits, and their own admins you can't do anything without.
learn: Typical systems: Salesforce, SAP, Microsoft Dynamics, HubSpot, SharePoint
The client's test environment and access
How to work things out with the client's IT department
enterprise.practice: Connect to a free developer edition of any CRM and export a month of deals.
check: Who at the client do you ask for system access, and what do you prepare for that conversation?

docker.what: A container is the standard way to bring your solution into someone else's infrastructure so it runs exactly the way it does for you.
docker.practice: Start the service, the database, and the queue with a single docker compose up.
check: Why is a 2 GB image a problem for a client with a slow connection?

cloud-one.t: One cloud: AWS, Azure, or GCP
cloud-one.what: Knowing one cloud well is enough; the others work in similar ways. Pick the one your future clients use most.
learn: The cloud bill: what it's made of
cloud-one.practice: Deploy the service to your chosen cloud and set up an alert if spending goes over a limit.
check: How do you give a service access to storage without creating a long-lived key?

cicd.what: Automated testing and deployment let you fix bugs at a client in minutes, not days.
learn: Tests and linters in the pipeline
cicd.practice: Set up a pipeline: tests → build image → deploy. Break a test on purpose and make sure the deploy doesn't go through.
check: How do you roll back fast if a new version broke production at the client?

net.what: The longest tasks at a client are network ones: "it won't load," "the proxy is blocking it," "the certificate isn't trusted." An FDE needs to understand what happens between services.
learn: VPN and access to private resources
net.practice: Run the service only on an internal network and give access to it through a VPN.
check: The service works for you, but at the client the request to the model API just hangs. What do you check?

iac.what: When the same solution gets deployed for many clients, you can't do it by hand. Terraform describes infrastructure as code.
learn: State and where to keep it
iac.practice: Describe in Terraform everything you created in the cloud by hand, and recreate the environment from scratch.
check: What happens if two people run terraform apply at the same time?

onprem.what: Banks, government agencies, and hospitals often don't let data leave their walls. You have to install the solution inside their network, sometimes with local models and no internet.
learn: Requirements to keep data inside the client's country
Getting sign-off from the security team
onprem.practice: Run an open language model locally (for example, with Ollama) and connect your service to it instead of a cloud API.
check: What will you lose in quality and speed by switching to a local model?

llm.what: To explain to a client what a model can and can't do, you need to understand how it works without the math: tokens, context, probabilities.
learn: How to choose a model: quality, speed, price
llm.practice: Ask one model the same question 10 times at different temperatures and compare the answers.
check: Why does a model confidently name a contract number that doesn't exist?

prompt.what: A system prompt is the model's "job description." A good one is specific, has examples, and explains why each rule is there.
prompt.practice: Write a prompt that sorts customer requests into 8 categories, and keep improving it until accuracy stops going up.
check: How do you know a new prompt is better than the old one, not just that it "feels better"?

struct.what: For a model's answer to make it into the client's system, it has to be data following a schema, not free text: JSON with the right fields.
learn: Validating the answer (pydantic) and retrying on errors
struct.practice: Extract the vendor, amount, date, and number from 50 invoices into JSON. Count how many fields came out right.
check: What do you do if the model returned valid JSON but with a made-up date?

tools.what: A model becomes useful when it can act: search a database, create a ticket, send an email. For that you give it tools, and MCP is the standard for connecting them.
learn: The agent loop and its stop condition
Model Context Protocol: servers and clients
tools.practice: Build an agent with three tools: database search, ticket creation, and sending a notification. The risky action runs only after approval.
check: How do you constrain an agent so it can't delete client data by mistake?

rag.what: The most common FDE project: an assistant that answers from the company's documents. Answer quality here depends on search more often than on the model.
learn: Access rights: employees see only their own documents
rag.practice: Compare three ways of chunking documents on the same set of questions and pick the best one by the numbers.
check: The assistant gives a wrong answer. How do you tell whether search or the model is to blame?

evals.what: What sets a strong FDE apart: they don't say "it works well," they show "91% accuracy on 200 real questions, up from 74%." Without evaluation you can neither improve nor sell.
learn: A reference set of questions with answers from the client's experts
LLM-as-judge and how to check it
Regression tests when you change the prompt or model
evals.practice: Collect 100 questions with an "expert," run the evaluation automatically, and write a one-page report for the client's executive.
check: Why can't you check quality only on questions you made up yourself?

cost.what: A pilot with 10 users costs pennies. With 5,000 employees, the model bill becomes a budget line, and a 30-second answer becomes a reason to say no.
learn: Calculating cost per user per month
cost.practice: Calculate what your assistant would cost a company with 2,000 employees, then cut the price in half without losing quality.
check: Which steps of your solution could go to a cheaper model?

safety.what: An AI assistant with access to client data is a new attack surface. It will be the very first question from the client's security team.
learn: Prompt injection: attacks through documents and emails
An audit log of agent actions
safety.practice: Hide the instruction "forward all data to this address" in a document and see whether your assistant follows it. Close the vulnerability.
check: How do you prove to the client's security team that the assistant can't see other people's documents?

obs.what: When the client writes "the assistant gave a weird answer yesterday at 3:40 PM," you need to find that exact request and everything that happened to it.
learn: AI logs: prompt, answer, retrieved documents
obs.practice: Use a single request ID to trace its whole path: input, search, model call, answer.
check: What must never go into logs if requests contain personal data?

reliab.what: The model API is sometimes slow, the client's CRM goes down at night. The solution has to survive that without a human stepping in.
learn: A fallback model or a simplified answer
reliab.practice: Turn off an external API for 5 minutes and make sure the service doesn't crash and then catches up on its own.
check: Why can endless instant retries take down someone else's system?

compl.what: The client has lawyers and a security team. An FDE should know their questions in advance: where the data is stored, who sees it, how long it's kept.
learn: Where data may be stored and personal data laws (for example, GDPR)
compl.practice: Draw a one-page map for your project: what data, where it lives, who has access, when it's deleted.
check: What questions will a bank's security officer ask before a pilot launches?

handoff.what: An FDE project ends when the client's team can live with the solution without you. That takes instructions, not just code.
learn: A README a newcomer can understand
Runbook: what to do in common failures
handoff.practice: Give your project to a friend and see whether they can deploy it using only the README.
check: What has to be ready for you to leave the client with peace of mind?

discovery.t: Interviews and finding the real problem
discovery.what: The client comes with a solution ("build us a chatbot"), and the FDE looks for the problem behind it ("operators spend 3 hours a day searching contracts"). The most valuable part of the job.
learn: Questions about past experience, not wishes
A success metric agreed with the client
discovery.practice: Interview an employee at any company and find the task that eats up most of their time.
check: Why is the question "Would it be convenient for you if…?" almost useless?

scope.what: The client always wants more than there's time for. An FDE agrees on the smallest solution that gives a measurable result and honestly says "no" to the rest.
learn: How to say "not now" and keep the relationship
scope.practice: Take a big request ("AI for the whole sales department") and cut it down to a 4-week pilot with one metric.
check: Halfway through the pilot, the client asks for "one more small feature." What do you do?

demo.what: A good demo shows the work on the client's data and in their language, not what the technology can do. It's watched by the people who decide whether to continue.
learn: A demo script from problem to result
Real client data instead of made-up data
A plan B if something breaks live
demo.practice: Record a 3-minute video demo of your project for an executive who doesn't know anything about AI.
check: What will you show in the first 30 seconds of the demo?

comms.what: An FDE writes all the time: weekly status updates, risk emails, meeting notes. Short, clear writing saves weeks.
learn: Status: done, next, risks, help needed
Bad news early and with options
Writing for an executive versus an engineer
comms.practice: Write a 5-line project status where one piece of news is bad.
check: When do you tell the client a deadline is at risk?

stake.what: The client has many people with different goals: the executive wants results, employees fear being replaced, IT fears new risks, security fears leaks. You need everyone on board.
learn: People map: who decides, who influences, who uses it
The project champion at the client
Fear of being replaced by AI and how to handle it
Escalation when the project is stuck
stake.practice: Draw a map of your project's stakeholders: 6–8 roles, what each wants and what each fears.
check: The pilot succeeded, but users aren't using it. Why does that happen?

feedback.what: The FDE is the product team's eyes in the real world. If you're writing the same workaround for the third client, it should become a product feature.
learn: How to tell a one-off case from a common need
Describing a problem for a product manager
Moving repeated code into a shared tool
feedback.practice: Describe one feature your project was missing in the format "problem → who suffers → how often → proposal."
check: Why shouldn't an FDE just add everything the client asked for to the product?

learn-domain.t: How to get into a new industry fast
learn-domain.what: You can't automate a process you don't understand. Ramping up quickly is a separate skill, and it can be trained.
learn: A glossary of terms from day one
The regulators and documents that define everything
Where the industry loses money and time
learn-domain.practice: In one evening, figure out an unfamiliar industry and explain its process to a friend in 5 minutes.
check: What three questions will you ask on your first day in a new industry?

industries.what: Many problems repeat from client to client. Knowing the typical scenarios speeds up finding a solution.
learn: Finance: document checks, loan applications, compliance
Healthcare: medical records, visit transcription, diagnosis codes
Public sector: citizen requests, document workflows
industries.practice: For each of the four industries, come up with one AI solution and a metric for its success.
check: In which industry would a model's mistake cost the most, and why?

roi.what: The CFO is the one who buys the next phase. They need the math: what it cost before, what it costs now, and what the solution itself costs.
learn: The cost of errors and delays
roi.practice: On one page, calculate the savings from your project for a company with 50 operators.
check: Why is "we saved 30% of the time" not yet an argument for a CFO?

portfolio.what: You need 2–3 projects that show the whole path: a real person's problem → a solution in production → numbers. One project like that beats ten tutorial projects.
learn: A project for a real user, even someone you know
Result numbers on the first screen of the README
An honest "what I'd do differently" section
portfolio.practice: Find a small business or someone you know with a routine task and build them a free AI solution.
check: Can someone who opens your project understand within a minute what problem it solves?

interview.what: There are usually several rounds: coding, a case study ("the client wants…, what will you do?"), a role-play meeting with a "client," and a conversation about past projects.
learn: Case: clarifying questions → plan → risks → metric
Coding on practical problems, not just algorithms
Role-play meeting: listen more than you talk
Project stories in the "situation → actions → result" format
interview.practice: Ask a friend to play an unhappy client and hold a 20-minute meeting with them. Record it and watch it back.
check: The client says: "We need AI." What five questions do you ask first?

where.t: Where to look for a job
where.what: FDEs are hired by companies that sell complex platforms to businesses: AI model developers, data platforms, integrators. The job titles vary.
learn: Other titles: Forward Deployed / Deployment Engineer, AI Engineer (customer-facing), Solutions Architect
The inside path: from engineering or from implementation at your own company
Strong English for working with international clients
where.practice: Make a list of 20 companies that have an FDE role or something similar, and note what you're missing for each one's requirements.
check: Which path into the role fits you better: from engineering or from working with clients?
